# Remote Recruitment to Diversify Infant Research Participation: Lessons From the Infant Vaccine Biepository

**Authors:** Eleanor Nicholson; Ritobhas Bhowmik; Emily Stonestreet; Ganad Neka; Audrey Mutoni; Amanda Michael; Tina Yi Jin Hsieh; McKenzi Thompson; Valerie Perrinez; Alejandra Barrero-Castillero; Ai-ris Y. Collier

**Affiliations:** 1Center for Virology and Vaccine Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Department of Neonatology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

To determine whether remote recruitment, electronic consent and at-home blood collection enabled enrollment of a geographically and socioeconomically diverse infant cohort in the United States (US).

We describe the demographics of 256 infants included in this analysis, drawn from 264 enrolled in the Infant Vaccine Biorepository (December 2022–April 2026). Participants were recruited via online advertising and electronic medical record messaging. Geographic distribution was assessed using US Census regions and Rural–Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes. Social vulnerability was characterized using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) at census tract and county levels, with nationwide rankings.

Infants were distributed evenly across the four US geographic regions; 9% resided in rural areas. Based on nationwide census tract-level SVI rankings, 39.8% of participants fell in the medium-high or high vulnerability categories. County-level SVI rankings indicated that 57.0% of participants fell in these same categories. Participants were 78% White and 20% Hispanic; 94.1% of mothers had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine.

Fully remote recruitment, consent and specimen collection enabled enrollment of infants from diverse geographic and socioeconomic backgrounds across the US. SVI and RUCA provide richer characterization of study populations than traditional demographic measures alone.

## Introduction

Research study populations often fail to represent target communities. Historically, women and minorities are underrepresented, and pregnant women are often excluded without justification [1]. Low-income individuals and those living in rural areas are also less likely to participate [2]. Although there has been a push to improve the diversity of clinical trials, drug trial enrollment still does not represent the United States (US) population. In 2024, participants across all trials were 70% White, 17% Asian, 8% Black, 19% Hispanic, and 5% American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, Other, Unknown/Unreported [3]. White participants remain overrepresented, while Black participants remain underrepresented. Many clinical trials lack adequate demographic information that captures socioeconomic status. Multiple longitudinal studies have found that less than half of US-based clinical trials report race and ethnicity, let alone socioeconomic information, of which less than 15% of studies report [4, 5].

Clinical research site location limits geographic representation. Traditionally, clinical trials and observational studies are conducted at urban academic research centers. In 2020, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reported that 50% of clinical drug trials took place in 1%–2% of zip codes [6]. Recruitment practices are often centered in academic institutions, which can be harder for some communities to access—thereby reducing the fairness of clinical trials [7, 8]. In vaccine research, this limitation is especially problematic because vaccine uptake could be lower and infections may have a greater burden in communities that might not be included as research participants [9]. Without adequate representation, generalizability of the results and the perceived efficacy of the data may both be reduced, and this may impact public trust of clinical trials and treatment options [10]. As a result, inequities may worsen because the standard of care is based on incomplete evidence.

Most clinical studies report race and ethnicity alone, which may not fully reflect the socioeconomic factors that shape health outcomes. United States mailing addresses can be utilized to determine the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) of the area where our study participants reside. SVI was developed by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to help identify communities particularly vulnerable to public health emergencies and disasters [11]. The measure includes four overarching domains: socioeconomic status, household characteristics, racial and ethnic minority status and housing type and transportation. Each domain contains specific subgroups such as health insurance status, education level, proficiency in English, or whether it is a single-parent household. Individuals living in high-SVI areas may reside farther from large academic research centers, and may also have lower income and face more significant barriers to in-person research, such as travel time, transportation costs and unpaid time off work [2, 12]. Individuals living in higher SVI areas are at higher risk for infectious diseases, and those populations may experience more difficulty in accessing clinical studies [9]. Another tool that can be used to assess a participant’s experience and level of accessibility to clinical trials are Rural–Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes [13]. These codes were developed by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to understand how rural or urban a census tract was based on commuting patterns to and from that area. Generally, RUCA codes 1–3 are defined as urban and 4–10 as rural. Researchers have leveraged RUCA to understand disparities in access to healthcare and how rurality may affect patient outcomes in clinical trials [14, 15]. One retrospective study exploring patient access to clinical trials in the rural Northwestern US found that participants were mostly from metropolitan areas as defined by RUCA, though 22% of participants were from rural areas [16]. Their conclusion was that as trials become more decentralized and offer more remote options, representation of rural populations will increase and improve the generalizability of trial results [16]. Our study’s use of remote recruitment, informed consent, data and specimen collection may mitigate barriers to research participation by reducing cost burdens and increasing representation by the communities most affected.

The Infant Vaccine Biorepository began in 2022 at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC). Initially, this study began at a single urban hospital and recruitment occurred in person; however, in identifying the need for diverse participant participation, the study quickly expanded across the US with the help of an online recruitment platform, electronic informed consent and remote capillary blood collection. The goal of the Infant Vaccine Biorepository protocol is to understand the magnitude and durability of passive immunity transferred from birthing parent to infant via the placenta by enrolling representative infants across the United States. This protocol was developed to reduce socioeconomic and geographic barriers to participation through a remote recruitment, consent and blood collection processes. The objective of this analysis is to characterize the geographic and socioeconomic diversity of our de-centralized research cohort using RUCA codes and SVI, which better capture infectious disease and health risk contexts than traditional demographic measures.

## Methods

### Study Population and Protocol

The study cohort includes infants enrolled through the Infant Vaccine Biorepository protocol from December 2022 to April 2026. Written informed consent was obtained from the legally authorized representative (LAR) of the infant. The Institutional Review Board at BIDMC approved this study (BIDMC IRB#2022P000765). Infants actively on study are 3 through 12 months of age. The infant cohort was recruited remotely using OpenClinica (previously BuildClinical), a digital recruitment platform that targets online study advertisements to potentially eligible participants. Eligible participants were pregnant people or people with infants under 13 months of age. Written consent was obtained from participants by phone using a remote e-consent platform (REDCap). Parents and guardians consented on behalf of the infant and had the opportunity to consent themselves to enroll in the study, as well. Once the participants had consented, we collected demographics, infant feeding method, vaccine and infection history by self-report through an online questionnaire on REDCap. We also captured the medical history, obstetric information and vaccine and infection history of the birthing parent. Parents sent infant samples to us at three time points using the Tasso+ Blood Collection device at three timepoints: 3–5, 6–8 and 10–12 months of age [17]. Prior to each sample collection, study coordinators contacted the parent or guardian for updated infant vaccine and infection history. Participants were provided financial compensation for each sample collection using gift cards distributed electronically by email.

### Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) Calculation

Participants provided a mailing address as part of study participation for sending and returning sample collection kits. The mailing address was also used to calculate their SVI. SVI can be assessed in four ways based on two dimensions: geographic level and comparison scale. SVI may be calculated at either the county- or census tract-level and compared either nationwide or within a given state. Here, we report both county- and census tract-level SVI data using nationwide rankings, meaning values are compared across the entire United States rather than within individual states. Although SVI values can be obtained from the CDC’s website by entering individual addresses, this approach is inefficient for large cohorts. Accordingly, all addresses were batch-geocoded to efficiently generate the SVI data. We used the United States. Census geocoding application programming interface (API) through the censusxy package in RStudio (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), the sf package for spatial processing and 2018 U.S. Census Bureau cartographic boundary shapefiles for all states represented in the study [18–21]. Street addresses were batch converted to latitude and longitude coordinates, spatially matched to census tracts and assigned corresponding Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) codes. Since FIPS codes can be linked to both county- and census tract-level SVI values, the FIPS codes we generated were merged with the CDC’s county- and census tract-level 2022 SVI datasets [22]. This process allowed us to assign SVI values to the whole study cohort included in the analysis.

### Rural–Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) Calculation

RUCA codes were developed by the USDA Economic Research Service to define the degree of urbanization and rurality of a census tract based on commuting patterns and size of nearby urban centers [13]. We utilized FIPS codes generated from the SVI calculation to assign each participant a RUCA code from the 2020 tract data. RUCA has a two-level classification system, with secondary RUCA codes incorporating additional commuting flow information. Secondary RUCA codes were not considered in this analysis. There are 10 primary RUCA codes, with 1–3 being Urban/Metropolitan and 4–10 being Rural/Nonmetropolitan. Primary level RUCA codes were assigned by linking census tracts with the tract-level 2020 RUCA dataset in R [13].

### Missing Data

Demographic information was obtained by self-report. Participants were allowed to decline response, and missing data from self-reports are reported as missing or unknown in Table 1.

Batch geocoding was unsuccessful for 66 addresses. These addresses were manually entered into the CDC SVI website to obtain SVI rankings. Census tracts may be split once their maximum populations are reached, which can result in changes to FIPS codes [23]. Because the cartographic boundary shapefiles used in this analysis were based on census information from 2018, whereas SVI values were taken from 2022 datasets, addresses located in census tracts that split between 2018 and 2022 could not be linked to SVI values if the original 2018 FIPS code was no longer valid. For example, a tract coded 7000 in 2018 may have been split into 7001 and 7002 by 2022 preventing direct linkage. In contrast, the CDC SVI website uses updated census tract boundaries that were not captured in the shapefiles used in this analysis, allowing linkage to current FIPS codes and corresponding SVI values. Also, 2 of the 256 geocoded addresses initially yielded unknown RUCA codes (i.e., neither urban nor rural). The corresponding FIPS codes were not present in the 2020 tract-level RUCA dataset likely because the census tracts split after 2020, and updated tract-level RUCA files were not available. We were able to designate the addresses as Urban or Rural using a ZIP code-based RUCA lookup tool; however, ZIP codes are less specific than census tracts [24]. Using the above techniques, we were able to interpolate all SVI rankings and RUCA codes for our cohort.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to report infant demographic information (Table 1). Continuous variables were summarized using the median and interquartile range (IQR) and categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Participants were categorized into 4 US regions according to Table S1. Rural versus urban residence was classified using 2020 RUCA codes linked to participant census tracts and reported in two categories with RUCA 1–3 assigned Urban/Metropolitan and 4–10 assigned. Demographic summary tables were generated in R. We report the proportion of participants in each SVI quartile as frequencies and percentages, with the least vulnerable in the lowest quartile and the most vulnerable in the highest quartile (Table 2). Vaccination status was summarized as number/total and percent, with maternal vaccination categorized as any maternal vaccine during pregnancy versus none, infant vaccination categorized as any reported infant vaccine versus none, and COVID-19 vaccination status summarized separately for the parent (Table 3). Descriptive spatial analyses and map visualization were performed in R using the ggplot2 package and a static bubble map template available online [25, 26]. The number of infants (n) and median SVI score for each state were summarized on both the county- and census tract-level. Bubble size represented the number of infants per state, while bubble colour represented the fixed SVI quartile in which the median SVI value for that state fell. Final nationwide maps were exported as high-resolution static images from R.

## Results

### Participant Characteristics

Two hundred fifty-six infants were included in this analysis (Table 1). Ninety-two percent of the infants were the result of a term birth (37 or greater weeks). One hundred twenty-seven (50%) were assigned female sex at birth, 78% reported white race and 20% reported Hispanic ethnicity. Infants were evenly distributed across the 4 geographic regions of the US, though 9% of the infants enrolled were classified as living in a rural area based on RUCA codes. Eight of the enrolled infants did not provide a mailing address and thus are not included in the data for this analysis. Despite the study title, ‘Infant Vaccine Biorepository,’ our study enrolled 23 of 256 reported receiving no vaccines in pregnancy, 20/256 reported no infant vaccines given in the first 12 months, and 12/256 (5%) infants had no reported maternal nor infant vaccination.

### Distribution of SVI

Based on nationwide census tract-level SVI rankings, 31.6% of infant participants were in the lowest social vulnerability quartile, 28.5% in the low-medium quartile, 19.9% in the medium-high quartile and 19.9% in the highest quartile (Table 2, left column). Based on nationwide county-level SVI rankings, 15.2% of infant participants were in the lowest quartile, 27.7% in the low-medium quartile, 24.2% in the medium-high quartile and 32.8% in the highest quartile (Table 2, right column). Maps were generated to illustrate the number of participants and average nationwide SVI rankings in each state based on participant census tracts (Figure 1) and county (Figure 2). Dark blue corresponds to the highest SVI quartile, and yellow corresponds to the lowest.

## Comment

### Principal Findings

Our infant recruitment methods have allowed us to reach infants from a range of geographic and socioeconomic backgrounds. The RUCA codes for our population suggest that most of our infants live in urban areas, while only 9% live in rural areas (Table 1). Based on nationwide census tract-level SVI rankings, 39.8% of infants in the study live in areas considered to be in the medium-high and high vulnerability category, and 60.2% are in the low and low-medium category (Table 2). Using state-level county SVI estimates indicated that even more (57%) infants fall within the medium-high and high vulnerability category.

### Innovation

#### Recruitment

Recruitment for clinical trials and observational studies has traditionally been done in person through connecting with providers or local flyering. Here, we recruit via an online recruitment platform that advertises the study on social media sites or through online searches.

#### Consent

Informed consent is usually obtained in person, where the investigator can adequately assess the participants’ understanding of the trial and ensure that the consent being obtained is truly informed [2]. However, since in-person consenting is often done at the academic, urban centre performing the study, it can create access barriers for individuals living far away or who face financial constraints. There are many options for remote consent. Here, we use REDCap E-consenting, which reduces the burden of travelling to a hospital while maintaining interactive, real-time communication with the participants.

#### Blood Collection

Participation in clinical trials often involves numerous in-person visits, sometimes just for blood draws or other specimen collections. The financial burden and scheduling constraints of in-person participation often mean individuals with low income, or those residing in high-SVI contexts, are less likely to participate. At-home blood collection reduces these opportunity costs and supports equitable participation.

### Strengths of Study

Despite the barriers in place that may have prevented families from joining the study, our remote recruitment and consenting methods made participation in the study more accessible. The use of SVI and RUCA as non-race/ethnicity metrics of social vulnerability is also a strength of the study. Most clinical trials publish limited demographic or socioeconomic data, making it challenging to understand the sociodemographic generalizability [4, 27]. Not only does our study report race and ethnicity, but we also report geographic location, rurality of the residence and social vulnerability as a closer estimation of socioeconomic status.

Using electronic gift cards as compensation via email, no social security number (SSN) was requested, reducing the barrier to participation by people who may be concerned about sharing their SSN or who do not have one. Many research studies in the US require a SSN to provide compensation for participants’ time, which limits who can participate [28]. Although our study is mainly focused on understanding vaccine effectiveness during pregnancy and in infants after birth, vaccination was not a requirement of this study, and some birthing parents and infants were not vaccinated (Table 3). Notably, 20 (8%) of our infants had no vaccinations reported (by their parent/guardian), 23 (9%) birthing parents did not report receiving a vaccine during pregnancy, and 15 (6%) reported never having received a COVID-19 vaccination. Our remote consent and sampling protocol was able to improve our outreach to medically relevant populations not always included in research, such as those who decline vaccination.

### Limitations of the Data

Although census tracts can provide a lot of information, using census tracts as a proxy for neighbourhoods, like addresses, may not be accurate on an individual level. The address at enrollment cannot represent mobility (moving to a different house or any experiencing housing instability) or capture specific experiences (likely culture, language). Furthermore, an address represents an area, not an individual, so some conclusions drawn from this data may not be entirely accurate in defining a participant’s experience, particularly for those who live in rural areas, which tend to be harder to classify and have more limited population data.

Another limitation of this analysis is that the most recent data on SVI is from 2022, so the SVI values may not reflect the vulnerability of today’s communities. As illustrated above, there is also a difference between SVI values when using census tract and county-level data. The counties are large geographic areas with populations in the millions and may inflate the vulnerability of certain residences, while census tracts reflect small communities that have a maximum population of 8000 individuals [23]. Once the census tract surpasses that number, the census tract splits into two new census tracts.

Although our cohort reflects substantial geographic and socioeconomic diversity, certain populations remain underrepresented. Recruitment advertisements (BuildClinical/Open Clinical) were available only in English, limiting participation among non-English–speaking families. In addition, enrollment required access to a smartphone to scan a QR code and submit interest, which may have excluded families with limited technology access.

## Discussion

When looking at the SVI and RUCA data for this study, it becomes clear that many of our study participants who are considered to live in highly vulnerable areas do not all live in remote or rural areas, but rather many live in urban centers. We are interested in continuing to widen the scope and reach of this study, particularly in rural areas of the US where there is less representation in vaccine research.

Since census tracts are smaller, more specific geographic units, the census tract SVI data is likely to be more representative of a participant’s vulnerability than county-based SVI data. Still, since we do not directly inquire about socioeconomic status (employment, insurance, or housing), we cannot draw definitive conclusions about the individual vulnerability of our individual participants. Furthermore, our race and ethnicity data show that our participants still do not match current US census data (Table 1). Although our sample does not represent the exact US distribution, it is more diverse than if we recruited from a single institution (or state).

Future steps include evaluating the diversity of vaccination history. Although we report vaccination status, we did not stratify the data by SVI or RUCA (Table 3). Understanding whether there is a relationship between SVI or RUCA and the likelihood to vaccinate could guide targeted public health interventions to improve vaccine uptake. We are also interested in evaluating participant proximity to healthcare centers. Some of the states represented in our cohort, such as Louisiana and Alaska, are among the most medically underserved in the country, particularly in terms of maternal and foetal health outcomes. As of 2024, half of Alaska’s counties were considered ‘maternity care deserts’, while Louisiana ranks 51st out of 52 states for preterm births [29, 30]. Our study design was able to capture data from infants living in some of the most medically underserved states in the country; however, future analyses are needed to identify whether our participants live in healthcare deserts.

## Conclusions

SVI and RUCA data show that the Infant Vaccine Biorepository recruitment methods have allowed us to include infants from a range of geographic and socioeconomic backgrounds. They also show that remote recruitment and sample collection can be particularly valuable for expanding representation in research studies. Equitable approaches to research should continue to be explored.

## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have shown incredible promise in medicine. While LLMs may be particularly useful in areas requiring extensive review of clinical records, their use remains limited due to their tendency to hallucinate and fabricate information. Hallucination issues, as well as their consequences, are exacerbated in low–probability, high–stakes scenarios such as rare adverse safety events or medical errors. We present SAFE–AI (Structured and Automated Framework for Explainable AI), a novel method for clinical decision making that combines the

strengths of clinical expert knowledge with LLMs in an ontology–driven model that minimizes hallucinations using strict rules. We test this method to identify medication errors in medical charts. We collected a sample of 18,402 lines of clinical information from 300 EMS clinical charts that were independently dually reviewed by two expert physicians for epinephrine adverse safety events (ASEs), with 96% inter-rater agreement. We tested SAFE–AI against these labels, achieving similar performance to human experts in detecting epinephrine overdoses with 97.9% accuracy, and 91.6% accuracy in identifying delays in epinephrine administration, greatly outperforming baseline LLMs models. Notably, some disagreements between clinicians and the model were found to be justifiable differences in judgment rather than errors. ## Author summary

LLMs have shown promise in analyzing clinical records but their use is limited due to their tendency to hallucinate and fabricate information. Misinformation could threaten patient safety and jeopardize trust. We developed SAFE–AI (Structured and Automated Framework for Explainable AI), which combines knowledge from clinical experts with LLM inference to detect adverse safety events (ASEs) with minimal errors. We tested our method in identifying medica­ tion errors in medical charts and compared results to reviews by expert physi­ cians. ## Introduction

It is estimated that over 250,000 adverse safety events (ASEs) occur annually in the United States among patients receiving medical care, resulting in more than 100,000 patient deaths [1–3]. ASEs, such as medication, diagnostic, or procedural errors; miscommunications; and healthcare associated infections, pose significant risks to patient safety in healthcare settings. The current standard for detecting ASEs is for expert clinicians to manually review clinical records [4,5]. Manual chart reviews are labor-intensive, slow, and costly. Consequently, ASEs are undetected and underreported, with over 95% of documented ASEs in medical records not being included in the official records, which hampers quality improvement and patient safety efforts [6].

Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) and particularly large language models (LLMs), have shown promise for augment- ing the abilities of healthcare professionals to analyze complex medical data. However, these models have limitations such as the propensity for LLMs to “hallucinate”, that is, to produce fictional or fabricated information that can be misleading and dangerous in clinical settings [7–9]. Recent studies have shown that their performance is highly conditional on the probability of the correct outcome [10]. As ASEs are relatively uncommon events, LLMs alone are not likely to correctly identify them. Even more troubling are some recent analyses of LLM robustness, showing the results of LLM requests are greatly dependent on the specific phrasing used [11].

LLM hallucination is most evident when the model is asked to perform reasoningbased tasks, but is greatly mitigated when limited to extracting information. This is demonstrated by the success of techniques such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [12], where the prompt is augmented with additional context from relevant

## Methods

Overview

SAFE–AI is structured in four major steps (Fig 1). Firstly, an ontology of epinephrine errors is defined by clinician experts using established clinical guidelines, and this ontology is converted into a directed graph. Secondly, an LLM is used to retrieve initial nodes in the graph - such as patient age and weight from an unstructured patient chart. Thirdly, a coding LLM translates the guidelines defined in the ontology into executable code. Lastly, a final prediction is made by executing the computational graph of all nodes from the initial inputs retrieved by the LLM to the final output node. SAFE–AI is sim­ ilar to RAG approaches as the LLM output is conditioned on contextual information, however, it separates this extraction step from decision-making. Thus, the only source of hallucination stems from the initial information extraction - a far sim­ pler task for LLMs to perform accurately.

Data collection

We acquired a sample of 5,089 pediatric OHCA patient care charts from 2014 to 2019 from a large nationwide provider of EMS transports using the National Emergency Medical Services Information System (NEMSIS) standard [15]. The study was approved by Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center’s Institutional Review Board (IRB#2022P000948). We randomly selected 409 charts to build a gold standard and test our system’s performance. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are shown in Fig 2. The final sample contained 300 charts and 18,402 lines of clinical information.

Clinical experts in pediatric Emergency Medicine and Critical Care independently verified inclusion status and de- ter­ mined presence of ASEs. Following a process described in previous studies [14,16,17], board-certified clinical experts used a validated PEDS tool to independently review medical records for ASEs. Reviewers underwent rigorous training and were required to have at least 80% agreement before they were allowed to independently review. Every chart was randomly assigned to two independent reviewers and disagreements were resolved by complete consensus.

Four clinical experts in pediatric Emergency Medicine and Critical Care verified inclusion status and determined pres­ ence of ASEs. Three of our four reviewers had served as the gold standard for severe ASE assessment in our prior work [16]; the fourth underwent training prior to review to ensure they had at least 80randomly assigned to two independent reviewers and disagreements were resolved by complete consensus.

We used Gwet’s AC1 to measure inter-rater agreement for epinephrine ASEs [18]. We have used this measure in previ­ ous studies [19] to overcome the “kappa paradox” [20], wherein the low prevalence of events, such as severe ASEs, could result in low scores despite high agreement among raters [18,21,22].

Data preprocessing

Charts in the National Emergency Medical Services Information System (NEMSIS) standard contain unstructured nar­ ratives and structured fields [15]. We used manually-crafted templates, such as “the patient weighs X kg”, to generate sentences from structured fields, following the strategy used by TabLLM [23]. Unstructured narratives were tokenized into sentences with Python’s Natural Language Toolkit [24]. The tokenized and templated sentences were combined into a single document and used as input for the LLM to perform information extraction.

Ontology of epinephrine errors

To demonstrate the capabilities of the SAFE–AI framework, we created an ontology to formalize epinephrine ASEs. In previous work [16,17] we created a classification system that defined epinephrine ASE as failure to administer when indicated, a delay to administer epinephrine within 10 minutes of arrival, and administering at least a 10x overdose or 50% underdose. In this work, we focused on the latter three. To build an ontology, we expanded these definitions with explicit criteria for prerequisites, and constraints.

Epinephrine is indicated in all pediatric pulseless cardiac arrest according to Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines published by the American Heart Association (AHA) [25]. Using expert consensus and rules developed in prior studies, we developed a specific ontology including specific time thresholds and erroneous doses that represent ASEs with the potential to negatively impact patient outcomes. We defined thresholds for severe ASE, mild ASE, and no ASE (Table 1), and included the generated ontologies for overdose, underdose, and delay in administration (Fig 1).

LLMs as zero-shot information extractors

LLMs, such as GPT–5, have demonstrated strong performance in extracting structured information from unstructured text. In this work, we leverage this capability while removing the need of LLM reasoning for clinical decision-making. Our design is motivated by the observation that extracting explicitly stated information (e.g., patient age, weight, medication doses, and timestamps) is a significantly easier task than performing multi-step clinical reasoning, which often requires strict adherence to thresholds defined in guidelines. In preliminary experiments, we found that LLM reasoning frequently led to inconsistencies and errors. More details in the Results section.

Therefore, we restrict the role of the LLM to zero-shot information extraction. Specifically, we use the model to identify and extract relevant entities defined by the epinephrine error ontology (Table 1) from clinical narratives. The extracted variables are then passed to a deterministic, rule-based system for ASE determination. To accomplish this, we combine the ontology with a template-based prompting system that dynamically generates queries and structures the outputs into JSON format. This design allows us to leverage the strengths of LLMs in parsing unstructured text while ensuring that clin­ ical decisions are controlled by explicit, verifiable logic.

Ontologies as computational graphs

Once the relevant inputs have been extracted from the source text with the LLM, a decision can be made with verifiable 93 logic. Using template-based prompting, a coding model (GPT 5.4 mini) is used during development to translate clinical guidelines into Python functions. Specifically, we generated the code offline and ran it in a sandboxed environment. Then, domain experts manually reviewed and validated the generated code to ensure fidelity to clinical guidelines, in addition to basic compilation errors or malicious code, and applied wrapper functions to handle errors and rounding of floating–point numbers. These verified functions are then fixed and reused across all experiments. This design promotes deterministic ASE detection.

When trying to determine an ASE, SAFE–AI selects the relevant output node in the graph and determines the required subgraph of relevant nodes with backward chaining instead of evaluating the full graph. Specifically, starting from the tar­ get node (i.e., ASE determination), we recursively traverse its dependencies in the ontology graph to identify all required ancestor nodes. This results in a minimal subgraph containing only the variables necessary for computing the target. Then, after initial nodes in the graph receive their values from the LLM extraction and are coerced to expected data types, the computational graph is executed from the input nodes to the output node. In case of missing inputs or any errors during execution, the program propagates the error and allows tracing it back its origin.

By treating the ontology as a computational graph where nodes represent concepts such as patient age, administered doses, or dosing ASEs, we ensure traceability of the decision-making. All the intermediate and output nodes have explicit computations that can be verified for accuracy, and only need to be defined once.

## Results

Clinician annotation and inter-rater agreement

A final sample of 300 pediatric emergency medical charts was reviewed by clinician experts. Gwet’s AC1 showed excel­ lent inter–rater agreement among clinical reviewers for evaluating epinephrine ASEs, with values of 0.85 for delays of ≥ 10 minutes to administer epinephrine and 0.96 for incorrect epinephrine doses.

We analyzed annotator behavior via pairwise confusion matrices and percent agreement across error categories (Fig 3). We observe that the agreement varied by type of ASE and, in general, reflected clinical ambiguity rather than random disagreement. For instance, in the case of epinephrine indication errors, clinicians agreed in most cases, with disagreements primarily occurring in “scoop-and-run” scenarios where rapid transport was prioritized over on-scene med­ ication administration. These cases frequently fell close to the pre-specified 10-minute threshold, leading to disagreement regarding whether the event constituted a failure to administer epinephrine versus a justified delay. Dosing error annota­ tions demonstrated high agreement, consistent with the high AC1 value reported above.

In this approach, all relevant information (clinical guidelines, task definition, and input case) is pro­ vided in a single prompt, and the LLM is asked to directly determine whether an ASE occurred or not. This corresponds to a single-step inference setting, where the model must internally organize the reasoning process without explicit intermedi­ ate structure. LLM with ontology baseline. In contrast, the second baseline incorporates a structured decomposition by following the ontology graph and predicting each entity in topological order, conditioning on previously inferred variables. These behaviors suggest that, while modern LLMs are highly effective at retrieving clinically relevant information from free-text narratives, unconstrained decision-making remains vulnerable to context fragmentation and overinter- pretation when performing final ASE determination directly from text.

Ontological prompting improves consistency but introduces conservative behavior

Incorporating ontological dependencies reduced several of the inconsistency patterns observed in the LLM-only baseline, particularly for overdose detection, where structured dependencies between patient weight, age, dose thresholds, and medication events improved logical coherence. Compared with the unconstrained baseline, the ontology-guided approach produced fewer spurious overdose predictions and more consistent internal reasoning.

However, the same constraints also introduced a more conservative prediction behavior. Error analysis showed that when intermediate ontology nodes were extracted incorrectly or left unresolved, downstream ASE determination fre- quently defaulted to negative predictions. This effect was especially apparent in delay detection, where small inconsistencies in timestamp extraction propagated through the dependency graph and prevented otherwise plausible ASE identification. These findings suggest that ontology-guided prompting improves structural consistency, but remains funda­ mentally limited by the probabilistic nature of LLM-based reasoning at the final decision stage.

SAFE–AI improves decision consistency through deterministic reasoning

SAFE–AI achieved the strongest overall balance between sensitivity and specificity by separating information extrac- tion from clinical decision-making. Unlike both baselines, SAFE–AI used the LLM exclusively to retrieve structured entities from the chart, while ASE determination itself was performed through explicit deterministic rule execution derived from clinical guidelines. This design substantially reduced hallucinated reasoning paths and improved consis- tency across complex temporal and dosage-related scenarios.

Qualitative review demonstrated that SAFE–AI particularly improved cases involving multi-step temporal reason- ing and cumulative dose interpretation. For instance, the framework correctly handled charts containing multiple epinephrine administrations interleaved with ROSC events, where the LLM-only baseline often failed to maintain a coherent temporal reference frame. Similarly, deterministic dose calculations prevented several overdose hallucina- tions caused by dupli­ cate narrative mentions or ambiguous documentation structure.

Error analysis

Error analysis revealed that the remaining SAFE–AI failures were dominated by ambiguity and inconsistency inher- ent to real-world clinical documentation. The largest source of disagreement arose from inter-reviewer variability, highlighting that a substantial subset of charts were themselves difficult to adjudicate even for expert reviewers. This finding suggests that some apparent model “errors” reflect uncertainty in the underlying clinical labels rather than algorithmic failure.

Among true model-related errors, most failures originated during information extraction rather than during ontology exe­ cution. In particular, formatting inconsistencies, incomplete timestamps, and conflicting documentation between structured and narrative chart components occasionally propagated incorrect or missing entities into the reasoning pipeline. Fewer failures were attributable to explicit logical reasoning errors, indicating that once the relevant clinical entities were correctly extracted, the symbolic execution framework remained largely stable and internally consistent (Table 4).

## Discussion

In this study, we proposed SAFE–AI, a framework that combines flexible language understanding with explicit sym- bolic reasoning grounded in clinical guidelines. We demonstrated the capabilities of SAFE–AI in detecting overdoses and delays in medication administration in clinical charts, and found that SAFE–AI shows strong overall performance and con­ sistently competitive or superior F1-scores relative to the evaluated baselines. While LLM-only approaches often achieved high recall, they were more prone to false-positive predictions and inconsistent reasoning behavior, particularly in complex cases. In contrast, SAFE–AI, which combines probabilistic information extraction with the deterministic execution of clini­ cal rules, resulted in more stable and interpretable behavior regardless of the underlying LLM model used and the format of clinical notes.

In spite of the advancements made by AI, manual chart reviews by clinicians remain the gold standard in ASE detection, particularly in out–of–hospital settings [5]. Focused reviews are the most accurate method, but are inadequate for timely intervention and can only be performed retrospectively. Because manual review requires substantial time and clin­ ical expertisechart are time and resource intensive, only a fraction of charts can realistically be reviewed, despite medical errors remaining a major source of morbidity and mortality in the United States [3,26–33].

Our results demonstrate the potential of SAFE–AI as a fast and scalable framework for ASE detection that could assist healthcare institutions to identify safety events shortly after chart completion, enabling earlier review and potentially timely corrective action. Moreover, SAFE–AI substantially reduces review time compared to expert manual abstraction. On average, specialized clinician reviewers required more than 10 minutes to review a two-page chart, whereas SAFE–AI completed the same task in under one minute. These findings suggest that symbolic clinical AI systems may help scale patient safety surveillance and quality improvement efforts while maintaining clinically auditable decision-making.

SAFE–AI is not without limitations. Although this study used a nationwide pediatric OHCA dataset containing vari­ ous EMS documentation styles and clinical scenarios, the evaluation was limited to 300 charts and focused specifically on epinephrine adverse safety events. Additional validation across broader patient populations and institutions will be required to fully characterize the generalizability of the framework. Furthermore, SAFE–AI currently depends on ontolo­ gies which require substantial domain expertise and manual development effort. While this explicit knowledge representa­ tion improves interpretability, extending the framework to additional ASE domains will require the creation and validation of new ontologies. Future work will focus on expanding the framework to additional clinical domains, evaluating performance on larger multi-center datasets and incorporating more advanced verification strategies

Although this proof-of-concept study was limited to a low-frequency event (epinephrine administration in pediatric OHCA), this high value intervention [34] is a common medical error in the out-of-hospital setting [35] and its detection continues to rely on manual chart review and human calculation [36]. We believe that clinically grounded frameworks such as SAFE–AI may provide a practical pathway toward scalable, transparent, and verifiable clinical AI systems capable of supporting patient safety and quality improvement workflows in real-world healthcare e‌‌nvironments.

## Abstract

## Background

Preclinical evidence identifies the serotonin transporter (SERT, encoded by SLC6A4) as an immune checkpoint on CD8+ T cells, with selective serotonin reuptake inhib­ itors (SSRIs) enhancing antitumor immunity in synergy with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy. Whether this translates into clinical benefit for patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is unknown. Using a target

trial emulation framework, we compared outcomes between SSRI users and benzo­ diazepine (BZD) users among patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving an ICI. Separately, in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which covers a different set of patients, we examined how SLC6A4 expression related to tumor immune-cell infiltration across cancers.

## Methods and findings

We emulated a target trial in the TriNetX federated electronic health record network (over 187 million patients), comparing SSRI with BZD treatment at first ICI administration under an intention-to-treat-analogue estimand. Eligible patients were adults with a solid tumor, a first ICI administration between 2015 and 2025, and a depressive or anxiety disorder recorded within the prior 365 days. Exposure required an active SSRI or BZD prescription overlapping the index date or starting within the preceding 90 days, not necessarily on that date. The

primary outcome was 2-year overall survival; 20 secondary outcomes across 4 mechanistic pathways were prespecified. Propensity score matching (1:1) on 49 baseline covariates yielded 1,567 pairs. Estimates are hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Transcriptomic analyses used TCGA (8,272 tumor samples from 8,172 patients, 20 tumor types). Among 3,134 matched patients, SSRI use was associated with lower 2-year all-cause mortality (23.5% versus 34.4%; HR 0.627; 95% CI [0.549, 0.716]; p < 0.001; E-value 2.57). Composite immune-related adverse events (irAEs) were more frequent with SSRI use (HR 1.162; 95% CI [1.039, 1.299]; p = 0.008), driven by thyroid dysfunction (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), without increases in hepatitis, pneumonitis, or colitis (all p > 0.09). Newly coded distant metastases were less frequent in the SSRI group (HR 0.629; 95% CI [0.487, 0.811]; p < 0.001), and the 3 prespecified negative controls (nephrolithiasis, cholelithiasis, cataract) showed null associations (all p > 0.76). All 5 individually analyzable SSRIs were associated with lower mortality (HR range 0.61 to 0.71). In TCGA, SLC6A4 expression was inversely correlated with T-cell inflammation in 13 of 20 cancer types, and this organ-level pattern matched that of organ-specific irAEs. The main limitation is residual confounding: performance status, a clinician’s rating of everyday functional ability that strongly predicts cancer survival, is not recorded in the network, and BZDs are prescribed in different circumstances from SSRIs, so the groups may differ in ways matching cannot capture. The TCGA analyses used bulk tumor tissue from patients not treated with ICIs, so they cannot localize SLC6A4 to particular cells or show that SSRIs alter the tumor microenvironment.

## Conclusions

In this study, SSRI use was associated with lower mortality and organ-selective immune activation compared with BZD use among ICI-treated patients with psychiatric comorbidity. Transcriptomic evidence supports biological plausibility. These findings warrant prospective evaluation of SSRI repurposing as an ICI adjuvant.

## What do these findings mean?

• SSRIs, which are already widely prescribed to people with cancer, were

## Introduction

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed treatment across multiple solid tumor types, yet only a fraction of patients achieve durable responses [1]. Depression and anxiety affect 20–40% of patients with cancer who receive immunotherapy [2] and are associated with worse treatment outcomes and survival [3]; both depression and serotonergic signaling are increasingly recognized to interact with immune function [4,5], underscoring the clinical importance of psychotropic medication choices in this population.

A landmark preclinical study by Li and colleagues [6] identified the serotonin transporter (SERT, encoded by SLC6A4) as an immune checkpoint on CD8+ T cells. SERT-mediated serotonin reuptake suppressed T-cell receptor signaling through the 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor (5-HTR) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, while pharma­ cologic SERT inhibition with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) restored intratumoral serotonin and enhanced antitumor immunity. In murine models, SSRI combined with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy produced synergistic tumor regression, establishing a direct mechanistic link between serotonergic signaling and check­ point blockade efficacy. These findings were independently supported by studies demonstrating enhanced immunosurveil­ lance through serotonergic mechanisms, including peripheral serotonin attenuation [7], pleiotropic SSRI-mediated immune enhancement [8], and tumor-associated macrophage modulation [9].

Because SLC6A4 encodes the molecular target of SSRIs and the principal route by which serotonin is cleared from the tumor microenvironment, it is the logical node linking serotonergic signaling to checkpoint immunity, and, among the genes of the serotonin pathway, the one most likely to be modulated by routine clinical SSRI exposure.

Clinical evidence for this SSRI-ICI interaction remains limited. Magagnoli and colleagues [10] reported a suggestive survival benefit with fluoxetine among Veterans Affairs patients receiving PD-1/programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) ther­ apy, but the analysis included only 34 exposed patients. Observational studies have linked emotional distress to worse ICI outcomes and reduced immune-related adverse event (irAE) incidence [11,12], but none have directly compared seroto­ nergic versus nonserotonergic psychotropic agents in a design that reduces confounding by indication through an active comparator. Large-scale clinical evidence with active-comparator controls and translational validation is therefore lacking, leaving the question unresolved between preclinical discovery and clinical application.

Because no randomized trial has compared serotonergic with nonserotonergic psychotropic agents in this setting, we used target trial emulation [13], an approach that applies the design principles of a randomized trial, namely explicit eligibility, defined treatment strategies, a common time zero, and a prespecified estimand, to observational data, reducing biases such as immortal-time and prevalent-user bias and making the intended comparison explicit when a randomized trial is unavailable. Because treatment was not randomly assigned, the resulting estimates remain associations rather than randomized comparisons.

Here, we report a target trial emulation comparing SSRI versus benzodiazepine (BZD) use among 3,134 propensity score-matched patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving ICIs, drawn from the TriNetX federated electronic health record network. The active-comparator design isolates the serotonergic mechanism by con­ trasting SERT inhibition (SSRI) against gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) signaling (BZD) in patients with equivalent psychiatric comorbidity. Twenty prespecified outcomes organized across 4 mechanistic pathways (immune enhancement, disease trajectory, BZD-specific harm, and negative controls) are used to discriminate among competing mechanistic explanations. To investigate the biological basis of these clinical findings, we examine SLC6A4 expression and immune microenvironment features across 20 solid tumor types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), including an organ-level cross-validation linking tissue-specific SLC6A4-immune associations to clinical irAE patterns. We asked whether the choice of psychotropic agent at ICI initiation is associated with subsequent outcomes, and hypothesized that, among patients with depression or anxiety who initiate an ICI, initiation of an SSRI rather than a benzodiazepine is associated with lower 2-year all-cause mortality, and that any such association is accompanied by an organ-selective increase in immune-related adverse events in the tissues where SLC6A4 expression tracks most closely with reduced immune-cell infiltration.

## Methods

Study design and data source

This retrospective cohort study used an active-comparator, new-user design [14] within the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, a federated electronic health record (EHR) platform integrating de-identified data from over 187 million patients

We compared outcomes between SSRI and benzodiazepine (BZD) users among patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who received immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy between January 2015 and December 2025. The active-comparator design reduces confounding by indication [15], as both groups carry psychiatric diagnoses and receive psychotropic treatment, while providing a mechanistic contrast between sero­ tonergic (SERT inhibition) and GABAergic (GABA-A agonism) pathways. This study is reported in accordance with the STROBE reporting guideline [16] (S1 Checklist) and the TARGET guideline for emulating a target trial [17] (S2 Checklist). The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Tri-Service General Hospital, National Defense Medical Center (TSGHIRB No. E202516013), with a certificate of review exemption.

The hypothetical target trial and its emulation are specified in full in the pre-specified analysis plan (S1 Protocol): eligi­ ble adults with a solid tumor and a documented depressive or anxiety disorder would be randomly assigned, at the time of first ICI administration (time zero), to initiate an SSRI or a benzodiazepine and followed for overall survival and prespec­ ified secondary outcomes under an intention-to-treat estimand. In the emulation, randomization is replaced by 1:1 pro­ pensity score matching on 49 baseline covariates, time zero is the first ICI administration, and follow-up, outcomes, and the causal contrast are operationalized from the electronic health record. Variables that a trial would balance but that are unmeasured here, notably Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite-instability status, are addressed through negative-control outcomes, E-values, and the sensitivity analyses described below. The target trial and its emulation are also specified component by component in S1 Protocol (Section 3) and shown schematically in Fig 1.

Study population

Patients were eligible if they met all of the following criteria: (1) age 18 years or older at the index date; (2) a solid malignant neoplasm (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification [ICD-10-CM] C00-C80) documented on or before the index date; (3) a first administration of any of the 13 US Food and Drug Administration-approved immune checkpoint inhibitors listed in S8 Table (including pembrolizumab, nivolumab, atezolizumab, durvalumab, and ipilimumab) between January 1, 2015 and December 31, 2025, which defined the index date (time zero); (4) major depressive disorder (F32, F33), generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1), or anxiety disorder not otherwise specified (F41.9) recorded within 365 days before the index date; (5) an active prescription for an SSRI or a benzodiazepine within 90 days before to 14 days after the index date; (6) at least 365 days of electronic health record data before the index date; and (7) at least 1 day of follow-up after the index date. The SSRI group comprised users of sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, citalopram, or fluvoxamine without concurrent benzodiazepine use, and the comparator group comprised users of lorazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, diazepam, temazepam, oxazepam, or chlordiazepoxide without concurrent antidepressant use (S8 and S9 Tables). Exposure was therefore ascertained from an active prescription in the window from 90 days before to 14 days after the index date: patients were new users of ICI therapy, and their psychotropic treatment could already have been in place before the first ICI infusion rather than starting on that day.

Patients were excluded if they had any of the following: (1) hematologic malignancy (C81-C96) at any time before the index date; (2) pre-existing autoimmune disease requiring immunosuppressive therapy; (3) HIV infection (B20) at any time; (4) a history of solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (Z94); (5) a schizophrenia spectrum disorder (F20-F29) or bipolar disorder (F30-F31) at any time; (6) systemic corticosteroid therapy at 10 mg or more of prednisone equivalent per day for 14 days or longer within the 30 days before the index date; (7) delirium (F05) within 30 days before the index date; (8) palliative care (Z51.5) within 30 days before the index date; (9) concurrent prescriptions for both an SSRI and a benzodiazepine overlapping the index date; or (10) a prescription for any non-SSRI antidepressant (serotoninnorepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, tricyclic antidepressant, or monoamine oxidase inhibitor) overlapping the index date. Mutual exclusivity of SSRI and benzodiazepine use was assessed at baseline, within the exposure window of 90 days

Outcomes

The primary outcome was overall survival (time from first ICI to death; 2-year window). Follow-up began on day 30 after ICI initiation, a prespecified 30-day landmark that aligns the survival window with the new-diagnosis outcome window and reduces immortal-time and early-death bias [19], and continued until death, last EHR contact, or day 730, whichever came first. The 2-year window was prespecified as the clinically relevant horizon for first-line ICI benefit and to harmonize follow-up across organizations with differing data maturity; a sensitivity analysis without time-window restriction was also performed. Twenty secondary outcomes were organized across 4 prespecified mechanistic pathways, which label the hypothesized mechanisms the study was designed to discriminate among and are not claims of established causation: path A (SSRI immune enhancement), path B (better disease trajectory), path C (BZD-specific harm), and path D (negative controls). Path A comprised 6 outcomes: thyroid dysfunction (new thyroid immune-related adverse event; E03, E06), a composite of new immune-related adverse events across 10 organ systems, a new systemic corticosteroid prescription, newly coded distant metastasis (C77, C78, C79), time to next treatment, and the number of ICI administrations during follow-up. Path B comprised 6 outcomes: an emergency department visit, unplanned hospitalization, palliative or hos­ pice referral (Z51.5), a new psychiatric diagnosis (F32, F33, F41, F43), opioid dose escalation, and suicidal ideation or self-harm (R45.851, T14.91, X71-X83). Path C comprised 5 outcomes: falls (W00-W19, R29.6), fractures (traumatic or osteoporotic fragility), delirium (F05, R41.0, R41.82), sepsis or severe infection (A41, R65.2, A49), and venous thrombo­ embolism (I26, I82). Path D comprised 3 outcomes without biological plausibility for differential SSRI-BZD association, serving as bias indicators: nephrolithiasis (N20), cholelithiasis (K80), and cataract (H25, H26). Unless otherwise specified, outcomes were ascertained between days 30 and 730 after ICI initiation; the per-outcome ascertainment rules and the complete code lists are given in S10 and S11 Tables.

As a progression-sensitive proxy, because radiographic progression-free survival cannot be ascertained in this net­ work, we defined time to next treatment as the time from ICI initiation to the start of a new systemic anticancer agent that was not part of the baseline regimen (chemotherapy, a protein kinase inhibitor, or a non-ICI therapeutic monoclonal antibody or antibody-drug conjugate), with continued or re-initiated ICI not counted as an event and death censored. To assess whether differential surveillance could account for differences in newly coded metastases, we also compared the per-patient frequency of cross-sectional imaging (computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography-computed tomography, and bone scintigraphy) between groups during follow-up.

Statistical analysis

Time-to-event outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier estimation with log-rank tests and Cox proportional hazards regression. The single primary outcome (overall survival) was prespecified; secondary-outcome p values are descriptive and unadjusted for multiplicity, and secondary findings are interpreted as hypothesis-generating. The proportional hazards assumption was tested using Schoenfeld residuals, and restricted mean survival time (RMST) is reported for the primary outcome. Palliative or hospice referral (p = 0.032) and venous thromboembolism (p = 0.042) violated it, so their hazard ratios are period-averaged effects. E-values were calculated following VanderWeele and Ding [20] to quantify the mini­ mum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would need with both exposure and outcome to explain away the observed result (S6 Table). Three prespecified sensitivity analyses were performed: per-protocol (N = 695 matched pairs), US-only (N = 1,450 pairs), and dual SSRI plus BZD versus BZD-only (N = 2,457 pairs).

The primary analysis estimates the intention-to-treat-analogue effect of SSRI versus benzodiazepine treatment at ICI initiation, consistent with the pre-specified analysis plan; the per-protocol analysis is a sensitivity analysis. We prioritized the intention-to-treat analogue because it matches the pre-specified estimand and does not require censoring at treatment switching, which on this federated platform cannot be corrected by inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting because patient-level data cannot be exported. TCGA pan-cancer transcriptomic analyses

To assess whether the serotonin transporter gene SLC6A4 associates with the extent of immune-cell infiltration across human cancers, we analyzed RNA-seq data from 8,272 tumor samples contributed by 8,172 patients across 20 solid tumor types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA); 100 patients contributed more than one tumor sample, and no patient appeared in more than one tumor type. Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) [21] was used to compute immune function scores (T-cell Inflamed Gene Expression Profile [GEP] [22], Cytotoxic Score [23]) and classify tumors into 3 immune phenotypes (Inflamed, Excluded, and Desert) [24]. Spearman correlations between SLC6A4 expression and immune scores were computed per cancer type with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Organ-level concordance was assessed by mapping tissue-specific SLC6A4-immune correlations to clinical organ-specific irAE hazard ratios for 5 organ systems with direct anatomical correspondence. A random-effects meta-analysis (restricted maximum likelihood estimator, Hartung–Knapp confidence interval) of SLC6A4 expression and overall survival was per­ formed across 18 evaluable cancer types. Full details are provided in the S1 Text and S13, S14 Tables.

To test whether the focus on SLC6A4 was justified rather than arbitrary, we extended the transcriptomic analysis to the entire serotonin pathway, computing the correlation of each of 20 pathway genes (the transporter SLC6A4, 14 serotonin receptors, the synthesis enzymes TPH1, TPH2, and DDC, and the degradation enzymes MAOA and MAOB) with three orthogonal immune signatures across the 20 tumor types, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The TCGA analyses are cross-sectional and use bulk tumor tissue from patients not treated with ICIs, so they cannot localize SLC6A4 to particular cells or show that SSRIs alter the tumor microenvironment.

## Results

Study cohort and primary outcome

From 187,237,420 patients in the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, 11,337 met eligibility criteria (Fig 2). After exclud­ ing 4,176 dual SSRI plus BZD users, propensity score matching yielded 1,567 pairs (Table 1). All covariates were well balanced (all SMD < 0.10; complete covariate balance in S20 Table). Median follow-up was 395 days (SSRI) and 349 days (BZD).

SSRI use was associated with significantly lower 2-year all-cause mortality compared with BZD use (368 of 1,567 [23.5%] versus 539 of 1,567 [34.4%]; hazard ratio [HR] 0.627; 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.549, 0.716]; p < 0.001; Fig 3). The proportional hazards assumption was met (Schoenfeld p = 0.825). The Kaplan–Meier estimated absolute risk difference increased from 3.0% at 3 months to 14.9% at 24 months. RMST analysis showed a 2.1-month difference in restricted mean survival time (SSRI, 19.1 months versus BZD, 17.0 months; S2 Fig). The E-value for the primary outcome was 2.57 (95% CI bound, 2.14).

Mechanistic pathway outcomes and organ-selective irAE

Twenty secondary outcomes were assessed across 4 pathways (Fig 4 and S5 Table; key outcomes summarized in Table 2).

In path A (immune enhancement), composite irAE incidence was significantly higher with SSRIs (771 of 1,567 [49.2%] versus 682 of 1,567 [43.5%]; HR 1.162; 95% CI [1.039, 1.299]; p = 0.008). Thyroid dysfunction was the primary driver (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), while hepatitis (HR 0.711; 95% CI [0.474, 1.065]; p = 0.096), pneumonitis (HR 1.023; 95% CI [0.734, 1.427]; p = 0.892), and colitis (HR 1.130; 95% CI [0.913, 1.397]; p = 0.260) did not differ significantly (S4 Table). New distant metastases were significantly less frequent with SSRI use among patients without baseline metastases (102 of 595 [17.1%] versus 142 of 569 [25.0%]; HR 0.629; 95% CI [0.487, 0.811]; p < 0.001). Time to next treatment, a progression proxy, was also longer with SSRI use (HR 0.876; 95% CI [0.811, 0.946]; p = 0.001; Tables 2 and S5).

In path B (better disease trajectory), SSRI users had lower rates of emergency department visits (HR 0.783; 95% CI [0.689, 0.891]; p < 0.001), hospitalization (HR 0.730; 95% CI [0.651, 0.817]; p < 0.001), palliative or hospice referral (HR 0.563; 95% CI [0.474, 0.668]; p < 0.001), and opioid escalation (HR 0.779; 95% CI [0.713, 0.851]; p < 0.001). New psychi­ atric diagnoses did not differ (HR 1.024; 95% CI [0.933, 1.124]; p = 0.610).

In path C (BZD-specific harm), delirium (HR 0.696; 95% CI [0.547, 0.886]; p = 0.003) and sepsis (HR 0.699; 95% CI [0.564, 0.866]; p = 0.001) were significantly lower with SSRIs. Falls (HR 1.014; 95% CI [0.797, 1.290]; p = 0.913) and frac­ tures (HR 1.028; 95% CI [0.830, 1.272]; p = 0.803) did not differ.

In path D (negative controls), all 3 outcomes showed null associations: nephrolithiasis (HR 1.042; 95% CI [0.767, 1.414]; p = 0.793), cholelithiasis (HR 1.043; 95% CI [0.764, 1.424]; p = 0.792), and cataract (HR 1.047; 95% CI [0.778, 1.410]; p = 0.761).

Mapping clinical irAE HRs to TCGA SLC6A4-immune correlations across 5 organs revealed concordance between reduced tumor immune-cell infiltration in the transcriptomic data and clinical immune activation (Fig 5D; S14 Table). ## Discussion

In this target trial emulation of 3,134 patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving ICIs, SSRI use was associated with a 37% lower hazard of death over 2 years compared with BZD use (HR 0.627; 95% CI [0.549, 0.716]). This mortality association was accompanied by increased immune-related adverse events, reduced metastatic progression, and a favorable disease trajectory including lower rates of hospitalization and palliative referral. Three null negative control outcomes, consistent results across per-protocol and US-only sensitivity analyses, and an E-value of 2.57 support the robustness of these findings.

The prespecified mechanistic pathway framework helps distinguish among competing mechanisms. Path A (immune enhancement) showed the most mechanistically informative pattern: composite irAE was significantly increased, driven selectively by thyroid dysfunction (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]) without significant increases in hepatitis, pneumonitis, or colitis. This organ selectivity suggests serotonergic modulation of T-cell activity concentrated in the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis [25,26] rather than generalized immune activation, and the absence of high-severity irAE increase provides a favorable safety signal. Reduced coded new metastases among patients without baseline metastases are consistent with, but does not by itself establish, an antitumor immune effect; comparable imagingsurveillance frequency between groups argues against differential detection; death is, however, a competing event for metastasis coding, and because we did not perform a formal competing-risk analysis this association is cause-specific rather than a subdistribution estimate. Path B (disease trajectory) showed consistently favorable results including significantly reduced hospitalization, palliative referral, and opioid escalation, reflecting both potential tumor control

All 5 individual SSRIs were associated with significantly lower mortality, supporting a class-wide SERT inhibition mechanism rather than agentspecific off-target effects.

The TCGA analysis addresses whether the inverse association between SLC6A4 expression and tumor immunecell infiltration is tissue-specific, a question with direct clinical relevance for predicting organ-selective irAE. Across 20 solid tumor types, SLC6A4 expression was inversely correlated with T-cell inflammation in the majority of cancers and associated with the Immune Desert phenotype, a pan-cancer pattern rather than a single-tumor observation. Critically, organ-level cross-validation showed that the thyroid, where the inverse SLC6A4-immune association was strongest, was also the organ with a significant clinical irAE increase (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), while tissues with no SLC6A4-immune association (liver, lung) showed no irAE increase. Colon showed a comparable transcriptomic correla­ tion (rho −0.326; FDR < 0.001) without a significant clinical increase (HR 1.130; 95% CI [0.913, 1.397]; p = 0.260). SLC6A4 was not independently prognostic in the pre-immunotherapy TCGA cohort, reinforcing that this axis becomes clinically relevant only in the context of checkpoint blockade.

These transcriptomic findings are best read as an independent, mechanism-oriented line of evidence rather than a demonstration that SSRIs cause the clinical associations: the TCGA samples are not from patients treated with SSRIs, so they support biological plausibility, not causation. Whether SSRI exposure actually shifts an immune-desert tumor toward an inflamed phenotype cannot be answered with cross-sectional data and would require a prospective cohort treated with ICIs with or without an SSRI, with paired pre- and post-treatment sampling and peripheral immune biomarkers, to estab­ lish such a conversion directly.

This study has several limitations. First, unmeasured confounders may introduce residual bias despite 49 propensity score-matched covariates. ECOG performance status, the most concerning potential confounder, is not captured in the TriNetX database; if SSRI users had systematically better functional status, this could partly explain the survival difference. PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite instability status were similarly unavailable. Established pharmacologic modifiers of ICI efficacy, notably baseline systemic corticosteroids [28] and antibiotic exposure [29], were addressed by excluding baseline systemic corticosteroid users and matching on baseline medication classes, although residual effects cannot be excluded. However, the E-value of 2.57 indicates that an unmeasured confounder would need a strong association with both exposure and outcome to fully explain the result, and the 3 null negative control outcomes [30] argue against systematic residual confounding. Second, ICD-10-based irAE identification lacks specificity for immune-mediated etiology [31–33]; thyroid events may include non-ICI-related hypothyroidism, and neuropathy codes capture both immune-mediated and chemotherapy-induced neuropathy. Nonetheless, this misclassification would bias irAE results toward the null, making the observed thyroid signal conservative. Third, the two drug classes are prescribed in different clinical circumstances: benzodiazepines are frequently given as needed for acute anxiety, insomnia, or distress around disease progression, so the comparator group may carry a worse underlying trajectory, a form of confounding by indication that would favor SSRIs. Several findings argue against this fully explaining the result, including preservation of the association across the prespecified sensitivity analyses, an E-value of 2.57, and an association that persisted against a comparator receiving neither agent (HR 0.753; 95% CI [0.605, 0.939]); the per-protocol estimate was directionally stronger (HR 0.575; 95% CI [0.472, 0.702]) but, being susceptible to informative censoring that cannot be corrected on this federated platform, is treated only as a sensitivity analysis; residual differences in psychiatric severity or care intensity nonetheless cannot be excluded, and the neither-agent comparison may itself be biased if untreated patients have milder illness or lower healthcare engagement. Fourth, SSRI prescription may proxy for integrated psycho-oncology care or more comprehensive healthcare engagement rather than a direct pharmacologic effect; however, the consistent association across all 5 individual SSRIs and the organ-selective irAE pattern are difficult to explain by differential care engagement

alone. Fifth, the TCGA analysis uses bulk RNA-seq data that cannot resolve cell-type-specific SLC6A4 expression on tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and the organ-level cross-validation involves only 5 data points, limiting formal statistical inference.

In conclusion, SSRI use was associated with lower mortality, organ-selective immune activation, and a more favorable disease trajectory compared with BZD use among patients with psychiatric comorbidity who were receiving ICIs. Tran­ scriptomic evidence that SLC6A4 expression is inversely associated with tumor immune-cell infiltration across human can­ cers provides biological plausibility. These findings support prospective evaluation of SSRI repurposing as an ICI adjuvant in a randomized trial, with immune-related adverse events and peripheral immune biomarkers as co-primary end points to confirm the proposed mechanism.

# Maternal RSVpreF and Infant Nirsevimab Immunizations Uptake During Respiratory Syncytial Virus Season

**Authors:** Ethan A. Litman; Tina Yi Jin Hsieh; Anna M. Modest; Kathleen Clarke; Melissa Dzinoreva; Valerie Perrinez; Esther Apraku Bondzie; Lydia Gallup; Eleanor Schonberg; Marjorie Rowe; K’ara Locke; Oluwaseyi Oginni; Robert Jones; Chloe A. Zera; Ai-ris Y. Collier

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts | 2Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 3Center for Virology and Vaccine Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts

## Abstract

This cohort study evaluates the use rate of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines to prevent RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease among infants.

## Introduction

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common virus predominately resulting in mild cold or flu-like symptoms for most adults and children.1 In older adults and infants, infection is a major cause of hospitalization and morbidity. In 2023, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Advisory Committee on Immunization Practice recommended the RSVpreF (Pfizer) vaccination during pregnancy to prevent infant RSV–related lower respiratory tract disease or nirsevimab administration to infants younger than 8 months born during the RSV season to a mother who is unvaccinated or vaccinated less than 14 days before delivery.2,3 These 2 new RSV interventions and historically disparate vaccine distribution in pregnancy presented an opportunity to study their simultaneous uptake.4 We described RSVpreF vaccination and nirsevimab administration patterns during the 2023 to 2024 RSV season.

## Methods

This retrospective cohort study included pregnant individuals and their infants delivered between September 1, 2023, and January 31, 2024, at an urban academic center. The Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center Institutional Review Board deemed this study exempt from review and waived informed consent because data use was for purposes of health care operations. We followed the STROBE reporting guideline.

Maternal and infant demographics and clinical information were abstracted from the center’s electronic health record. Race and ethnicity were self-reported (eTable in Supplement 1) and collected to ensure generalizability of findings. RSVpreF and nirsevimab immunizations were available at the beginning of RSV season. RSVpreF and nirsevimab administration timing, location, and ordering clinician were abstracted from a statewide immunization portal maintained by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health. Analysis was performed using Python 3.13.1 (Python Software Foundation).

## Results

During the study period, 1899 pregnant patients (median [IQR] age, 33.9 [30.9-36.8] years) were admitted for childbirth. Of 1955 associated fetuses or neonates, 15 were excluded due to abortions and perinatal demise, leaving 1940 live births (median [IQR] gestational age, 39.1 [37.7-39.9] weeks) for inclusion. Most mothers received care in an academic (952 of 1899 [50.1%]) or private practice (721 [38.0%]) and had commercial insurance (1290 [67.9%]). The preterm birth rate was 12.5% (236) at less than 37 weeks and 3.0% (57) at less than 32 weeks (Table).

Most live-born infants received RSV protection (1063 of 1940 [54.8%]), of whom 696 (65.5%) received protection after birth. Thirty infants received both maternal and newborn protection, of whom 19 (63.3%) appropriately received nirsevimab, with birth occurring less than 14 days after maternal vaccination. The preterm birth rate observed for mothers who received RSVpreF was 8.2% (32 of 389).

At RSV season end, 389 patients (20.5%) received RSVpreF and 665 infants (35.0%) received nirsevimab. The proportion of infants receiving RSV protection increased each month (eg, 27.1% in September 2023; 77.7% in January 2024) (Figure, A). Differences in maternal vaccine rates across race and ethnicity categories persisted throughout the RSV season; however, race-based disparities in nirsevimab administration decreased (Table and Figure, B). RSVpreF was administered mostly at outpatient commercial pharmacies to mothers with commercial insurance (202 of 308 [65.6%]) or government insurance (42 of 81 [51.9%]). RSVpreF vaccination rates improved over time through increasing administration at both prenatal offices and outpatient pharmacies (Figure, C). Most newborns were immunized during the birth hospitalization (Figure, D).

## Discussion

Overall, 20.5% of mothers and 35.0% of infants received RSV immunizations, consistent with previous CDC report5 but lower than the 35% maternal vaccination rate reported in a New York health system.6 Increases in both pharmacy- and office-administered immunizations during hospitalization were associated with enhanced RSV protection. Disparities in maternal, but not infant, vaccination persisted throughout the study.

Study strengths were the large, diverse patient population with varied practice settings and payer types. Immunization data were uniformly collected using a statewide mandatory vaccine reporting data source. Study limitations were lack of data on patient decision-making regarding vaccination and potential for vaccination-status misclassification. Future research should focus on systemic reasons for nonvaccination. Health care systems should focus on infant immunization during the birth hospitalization to increase equity.
